title: SCE stdout manifest (wire schema v1)
description: The single JSON line sce-codegen writes to stdout on success. One record per invocation, never pretty-printed, terminated by a single newline. Emitted only when the process exit code is 0 — on failure stdout is empty and the NDJSON diagnostic on stderr is the sole signal. The `kind` field names the subcommand that produced the record so a consumer branches before reading subcommand-specific fields. Authoritative producer is sce-build/src/manifest.rs; the prose contract is SCE_ERROR_CONTRACT.md §10. Consumers MUST ignore unknown fields: any purely additive change is compatible with v1 and does NOT bump `v`. The stability status of this surface lives in this header alone, not in the payload — see SCE_WIRE_CONTRACTS.md for the shared deprecation policy across SCE wire surfaces.

v.description: Manifest schema version. Always 1 for this revision. Additive field growth does NOT bump this.

kind.description: Which subcommand produced this manifest. Consumers branch on this before deserialising into a subcommand-specific shape. Kept in lockstep with the Rust ManifestKind enum by manifest.rs::tests::json_schema_kind_enum_matches_rust_source_of_truth.

generator.description: Commit of the sce-codegen build that produced this record, or "unknown" when the build had no git checkout to read (vendored crate, release tarball). The crate version is frozen pre-1.0 and identifies nothing on its own, so the pattern excludes it: a required stamp whose shape is unconstrained is discharged by a value that names nothing. Same field, same pattern, on every surface a consumer reads without a second invocation (SCE_WIRE_CONTRACTS.md policy 2).

artifacts.description: Every file written during the run, in emission order. Entries are objects rather than bare strings so the shape can grow additively (size, hash, artifact_kind) without a v-bump. Always empty for kind="check", which is that subcommand's whole contract: it reaches the same verdict as generate while writing nothing.

needs_script_engine.description: Whether the compiled machine embeds ECMAScript requiring a runtime script engine.

needs_event_scheduler.description: Which driving entry point the emitted machine requires of its host: true means the runtime's tick(), false means step() is enough. tick() drains the delayed-send scheduler and ticks invoked child sessions; step() does neither, so a machine with a <send delay> / <cancel> or a session-bearing <invoke> that is driven by step() alone loses those events with no error and no diagnostic. Always present, so false is an answer rather than an absent field.

script_engine_causes.description: Why needs_script_engine is true — one record per construct that forced the engine in. Present exactly when the flag is true; omitted (not []) otherwise, so a pure-static manifest carries no extra bytes. A non-fatal degradation report: generation succeeded, but the output is weaker than the author may have intended.

script_engine_language.description: Which language the script engine this machine needs must evaluate. Present when needs_script_engine is true AND the run targeted a single backend; absent on a multi-backend run (check sweeps every language and they do not agree). needs_script_engine says a host must supply an engine; this says what kind, and the two are not the same question, because a document declaring datamodel="ecmascript" is not necessarily evaluated as ECMAScript. THIS IS PER-BACKEND. Rust, Go, Python and C11 receive Lua that SCE's ECMAScript frontend lowered at generation time, so their engine must evaluate Lua. C++ and Kotlin receive the author's ECMAScript source and hand it to the injected engine as it stands — their generated code takes its engine by injection and cannot know at generation time which one arrives — so their engine must evaluate ECMAScript, and both default to one (SCE_SCRIPT_ENGINE=quickjs, W3CTestBase.DEFAULT_ENGINE=rhino). This description previously said the opposite ("Not per-backend ... every language's generated machine evaluates the same translated source") and the enum admitted only "lua", so a C++ or Kotlin host obeying this field supplied a Lua engine for a machine that speaks ECMAScript to it. See docs/SCE_LUA_TRANSLATION_SEAM.md for the per-backend table and docs/SCE_ACCEPTED_SUBSET.md §B.2 for what the lowering covers.

needs_host_processor.description: Whether any <send> or <invoke> in this run names an Event I/O Processor or invoker type this build has no lowering path for. Third member of the family needs_script_engine and needs_event_scheduler belong to — all three answer what the host has to supply, and the generator settles all three while compiling. true does not mean the document is wrong: W3C SCXML 6.2 and 6.4.1 define the unsupported-type case, so the site raises error.execution and a build relying on that refusal is a legitimate reading. What the flag reports is that the refusal will happen, at a state the host may not enter for hours, with nothing before this record to say so. Only a literal `type` is judged; a `typeexpr` has no build-time value and is checked by the generated code at runtime. Always present, so false is an answer rather than an absent field.

host_processor_causes.description: Why needs_host_processor is true — one record per site naming a type this build has no path for. Present exactly when the flag is true; omitted (not []) otherwise. Non-fatal: generation succeeded, and the emitted code refuses these sites at runtime exactly as the specification requires.

host_processor_types.description: Event I/O Processor types this build was told the host serves (--host-processor). Omitted when none were declared. Reported because the declaration and the runtime registration are two halves made in two different places — the build command and the host's startup code — so publishing the build's half lets a consumer check the pair instead of meeting the mismatch as an error.execution at run time. A declared type is absent from host_processor_causes: that is what declaring it does.

host_invoker_types.description: <invoke type="..."> values this build was told the host can run (--host-invoker). Omitted when none were declared. A separate field from host_processor_types because they are separate contracts: delivering an event is not the same capability as running an invoked process with a lifecycle (start, cancel, done.invoke), so a consumer checking its registrations has two lists to check. Not routed to a host invoker: parent-to-child <send target="#_invokeid">, autoforward, and <finalize> — those are mechanics between two SCXML sessions.

unreadable_variables.description: The typed <data> declarations this run emitted no typed reader for, and why (W3C SCXML 5.3). Omitted when every typed declaration got one. A reader that is not there looks, from the host's side, like one the generator forgot or a name the host misspelled, so the absence is published with its cause. Decided the same for every backend: a name that no backend's escape can give a reader gets none in any, so a check sweep and a single generate report the same list.

holder.description: The object a transform keeps its previous() values in, by the names the target backend gave it. Present exactly when the run generated one; omitted otherwise, and omitted on a run spanning several backends, whose names differ. A transform is pure functions unless an output reads a field through previous(), and then the host must drive it through the holder — construct one, call update once per activation, reset to start again — because only the holder keeps what the next activation reads. Which of the two a document is follows from its content, not its sce:kind.

rejected.description: Present only when the input triggered a W3C-spec rejection and stub files were written in place of generated code. Absence means clean generation.

deploy.description: Declarations read out of --deploy that SCE records without acting on. Omitted whole when the run had no deploy or the deploy declared none of them.

formatter.description: The external formatter that shaped the emitted artefacts, as the run resolved it. A formatter is an input of the bytes like the generator, so a run that used one names it; its major is pinned by the generator (clang-format 19 for C++). Omitted when the run formatted nothing (--no-format, or no C++ emitted).

languages.description: Per-language verdict. Present only for kind="check": one entry per language the run checked, in the canonical language order. Names the backend axis explicitly so a consumer never has to infer, from a single exit code, whether a document was refused on its own merits or only by the backend it happened to be generated for.

path.description: Path of the written file, as the invocation named it.

kind.description: Stable kebab-case discriminator for the construct that forced the script engine in. Deliberately not an enum: consumers dispatch on this and MUST tolerate values added by later revisions.

state.description: Owning state, for causes anchored to a state or a transition.

var.description: Datamodel variable id, for the <data> initializer cause.

kind.description: Stable kebab-case discriminator for the element that named the type: "send-type" or "invoke-type". Deliberately not an enum: consumers dispatch on this and MUST tolerate values added by later revisions.

processor_type.description: The type attribute verbatim, so the record names the URI that was refused rather than only the element that carried it.

reason.description: Stable kebab-case discriminator: "type-disagreement" (the name's declarations disagree about its type), "not-an-expression" (a json reader must name the variable in an expression and this name cannot be one), "keyword" (a keyword of language that the language gives no way to escape), "not-an-identifier" (the spelling is not an identifier in language), "member-collision" (the spelling is a member the generated type already carries), "duplicate-spelling" (another variable, named in with, folds to the same spelling). Deliberately not an enum: consumers MUST tolerate values added by later revisions.

language.description: The first backend whose spelling could not be used. Absent for the two reasons about the document rather than a language.

spelling.description: The refused spelling in that backend.

outputs.description: The record one activation returns: every output, by name.

new.description: What makes a holder whose kept values are at their fields' sce:initial: the type itself where a constructor is spelled by its type's name (C++, Kotlin, Python), the associated `new` on Rust, `New<Type>` on Go, and on C11 `<prefix>_init`, which fills a holder the caller owns.

reset.description: Every kept value back to its field's sce:initial.

restored.description: What makes a holder whose kept values of RETAINED fields are the ones the host stored, and every other at its field's sce:initial. It takes the stored values in the holder's cell order: inputs, then outputs, each in declaration order. Present only when a field read through previous() is also sce:retain: a value that outlives the program is the host's to keep, and this is where the host hands it back.

spec.description: The spec rule that rejected the document, e.g. "W3C SCXML 5.8".

static_analyzer.description: Which commercial analyzer the deployment declares it relies on. SCE never verifies the claim — carrying it here is the whole of SCE's part. Kept in lockstep with the Rust StaticAnalyzer enum.

version.description: The version the formatter reported, e.g. 19.1.1.

language.description: Backend the verdict applies to. Kept in lockstep with the Rust Language enum's wire names.

status.description: "ok" when this backend would generate the document, "rejected" when it would refuse.

code.description: Diagnostic code of the refusal, present exactly when status is "rejected". Same vocabulary as the diagnostic wire's `code` field, so a consumer routes a check refusal through the repair path it already has.
